claims.text: The proposed intervention is sequential aging at 600 °C for several hours followed by aging at 700 °C for several hours.
An as-cast or conventionally annealed AlCoFeNi-based alloy is expected to begin in a relatively uniform, typically ordered-B2 single-phase state.
A several-hour anneal at 600 °C will nucleate fine precipitates in AlCoFeNi.
A subsequent several-hour anneal at 700 °C will grow and stabilize the precipitates nucleated at 600 °C.
The two-step aging treatment will produce a hierarchical microstructure of fine, coherent precipitates dispersed in the AlCoFeNi matrix.
Fine coherent precipitates in this alloy will act as domain-wall pinning sites.
Pinning by the precipitates will impede domain-wall motion during magnetization reversal.
Impeded domain-wall motion will increase the energy barrier for reversal and thereby raise coercivity.
The two-step-aged sample will have a measurably higher coercive field than an as-cast, conventionally annealed, or single-step-treated baseline measured under identical conditions.
The coercivity increase may be accompanied by a reduction in saturation magnetization.
Composition and annealing temperature affect the length scale and nature of phase decomposition in AlCoFeNi-related alloys.
Large deviations in alloy composition or processing may prevent the same microstructural evolution and coercivity response.
Aging duration and precipitate size and distribution will influence the final magnetic properties.
The predicted effect is conditioned on reproducibly controlling the two aging temperatures and durations and using identical room-temperature hysteresis protocols.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant coercivity increase over the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe fine coherent precipitates after the two-step treatment would falsify the proposed intervention-to-mediator relationship.
